Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training people in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades.  Perhaps you've wanted to attend but could not get permission for travel to Scotland or the scheduling of workshops in August conflicted with your field work.

We are offering the training workshop in 10 two-hour blocks in early January.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The block will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud"☁️; both free software tools.  You will need accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://rstudio.cloud before the course begins.

Registration for the first offering of this training filled within a week of advertisement.  Persons on the wait list for the first offering have already filled half of the available places.  I suggest you register and pay without delay.

Important details:

    Workshop dates and time: 06 - 17 January 2020; 1800-2000 UK time (1300-1500 EST, 1000-1200 PST,  0900-1100AKST) 🕰️
    Registration deadline: 28 November 2019📅
    Enrolment limit: 10 - five participants from the wait list for November have already registered, so there are no more than five places remaining
    Cost: 170 British pounds (roughly $205 at current exchange rates)💵
    What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

Further details are available at the CREEM website:

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-live-online-workshops/

At this page you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where you a) register and b) make payment.

Feel free to contact me with questions.  We expect to offer this training again in spring 2020 if January timing does not suit you.  Future offerings may use the Distance for Windows software if there is sufficient demand.  The interactive workshops do not replace face-to-face distance sampling workshops that will be held in August 2020.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dayrone,

When we check our data in 'Distance', it shows us sorted data on the basis of 'transect label' and then 'Effort length'. When you are leaving any column blank in your data file, you should keep different 'Transect ID' for no observations in case of zero observations throughout the effort and then put 'Effort length' in another column. You can check whether Distance is considering your blank observations by checking the total effort length in the last. If your effort length is what you are expecting, means Distance is reading your data correctly.

Hope this helps!

Regards
Deepti

Hi! thank you very much for the advice Deepti, but fortunately the problem was very simple and could be solved just knowing a particular tha I did not specified cause I didn't think it was correlated. Eric clarified it to me in a mail: what I didn't say is that I walked along the transects more than once and so I did replicates. In order to take account of these, I put all the observations of the three replicates for every transect one after the other in Distance, but I multiplied by a factor 3 the lenght of the transect so as to maintain the effort of sampling. Given this, the software did not put in the data the "no observation" days because they are not important if in at least one of the three replicates I have recorded something. What Distance did in fact was leaving a blank space only for those transect completely devoid of records in all the three replicates.
Thank you again for your answer!
Dayrone

messages.body_plain:
Section 9.4 of Buckland et al 2015 gives a good theoretical explanation of converting from cues per unit time per area to density of clusters/individuals.

How is this done practically in the R Distance package? I don't see any arguments in the ds() function. Whilst I assume you could scale manually using a cue rate, I'm not sure how to deal with the confidence intervals produced by ds() when doing so. Vu et al. 2017 do something very similar in their paper A distance sampling approach to estimate density and abundance of gibbon groups, but using Distance for Windows.

For more details on my specific case: I wasn't involved in survey design, but I am analyzing point count data from gibbon groups, surveyed for around 5 hours each morning for 3 days from a number of sampling points. Distances to calling groups are estimated without triangulation. I have produced detection functions using the call data. Ideally I would use a cue rate from the literature, or calculate a cue rate from this data, and use that to adjust.

It is in a subsequent calculation where density of cues is converted to density of animals producing those cues.

messages.subject: Weighted Standard Error
messages.subject_clean: Weighted Standard Error
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling group,

I have two different density estimates based on line transect sampling for a species within two different parts of a Protected Area (total area ~2,000km2), part 1 is the “outer core” (~1500km2) and part 2 is the inner core (~500km2) which is embedded in the outer core. The areas do not overlap.

The density estimate for the outer core was based on a line transect survey in 2010, and that of the inner core in 2011. The scientist used a pooled detection function as the encounter rate was very low for the species, thus the same detection function was used for both density estimates. The density was higher in the inner core compared to the outer core. The survey effort was also higher in the inner core as the same number of transect lines (~40) was used in a smaller area.

I would now like to obtain a density estimate for the entire PA by combining the two density estimates. The reason I need this single density estimate is because subsequent surveys in the PA randomly sampled the entire PA and used one density figure for the entire PA. I would like to compare this latter figure to the baseline.

I am considering two different approaches.

Approach 1: Using an area-weighted mean density (i.e. (D1*1500+D2*500)/2000 = Dtotal). This option has my preference as it is quick and easy, I need the answer fast, and I may have difficulties finding the original datafiles. However, my question is here: how to calculate the (weighted) standard error?

Approach 2: Re-do the original analysis. This is obviously more time-consuming and it may be hard to replicate original works exactly as some information is missing. Also, I would then have a non-random survey design where a part of the area has been purposefully sampled much more intensely + and the survey year is not-random, all seems to violate important assumptions.

I’d greatly appreciate recommendations J

Best wishes

Milou

messages.body_plain:
A textbook formula under the condition of independent random variables. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances.  When those sums are weighted, the weights need to be squared.

Note, this is all couched in terms of variance.  What you have for your stratum-specific estimates are likely the standard errors of the stratum-specific density estimates.  You'll need to convert them to variances by squaring. The result you derive from the above formula will be a variance of the weighted sum.  You'll want to square root it.

However, all of the above only holds if the X_i values are independent, which they are not in the scenario you describe (the density estimates for the two areas share a common detection function).

Variance estimation for the situation you describe is laid out in detail in Buckland et al. (2001) Section 3.7.1, pages 89-90.  Let me know if you are unable to locate a copy that provides explicit formulas for your situation.

You are on the right track.  Let me address your points:

1)  For Section 3.7.1 you can treat f(0) as equivalent to h(0).
2)  Given you have an estimate of ESW and a measure of its precision; work with CV as the measure of precision.  CV is defined as SE(estimate)/estimate.   The CV of ESW is identical to CV of f(0).  Use that knowledge to solve for var(f(0)).

Total effort (summed across all transects) is sum of effort.  You are right "k" is the physical number of transects, not multiplied by number of times walked.

What are the consequences of creating segments greater than the truncation distance when creating a DSM? If I increased the segment width to 200 m, it would mean I effectively have complete coverage of the study area by the segments, is this an issue when performing DSM?

Any advice is much appreciated.

Regards,
Luke.

That all seems quite thorough to me.  I don't expect there to be much difference between the confidence intervals produced by 3.95 and 3.71. Is binning my data an appropriate why of remedying my delimna? And if so, how should I make my bin classes so that I'm losing as little information as possible.

Thank you very much to anyone who can offer some insight on this issue!

messages.body_plain:
Adrienne

I'm not an expert on detecting chimpanzee nests, I'm guessing they are in trees.  I suggest it might be more difficult to detect nests when viewed from underneath than when viewed more from the side.

If you analyse the data as exact distances (as the data were collected), using a model with a shoulder such as the half normal, then you may  have a detection function shape that compensates for the nests missed close to the transect: it will miss the first histogram bar high and perhaps fit well for the remaining detections.  But your goodness of fit metrics may suggest poor fit.

You can choose to bin your data for the purpose of fitting a detection function.  However the choice of bins is subjective--there are no guidelines for how to do this.  In particular, using AIC comparisons for different binning choices or truncation distances is invalid, because AIC comparisons are only valid when exactly the same data are fitted to models.  There is also no mandate that all bins are of the same width.  I suspect a complete analysis of the data will likely truncate detections beyond, say 50m as those detections have little information about the shape of the detection function near the transect.

As you can see, there are many types of decisions associated with your questions, but little in the way of objective procedures to assist you. I'm willing to look at your histogram if you wish to send it to me off-list.

Adrienne, just adding to what Eric has said, you can’t use AIC to compare binned and unbinned analyses – the AIC values are not comparable.

I guess another possible cause of a lack of detected nests near the transect is if the transect tends to avoid trees that might hold nests, for example, if it follows a road or track. Steve Buckland

Adrienne

I'm not an expert on detecting chimpanzee nests, I'm guessing they are in trees.  I suggest it might be more difficult to detect nests when viewed from underneath than when viewed more from the side.

If you analyse the data as exact distances (as the data were collected), using a model with a shoulder such as the half normal, then you may  have a detection function shape that compensates for the nests missed close to the transect: it will miss the first histogram bar high and perhaps fit well for the remaining detections.  But your goodness of fit metrics may suggest poor fit.

You can choose to bin your data for the purpose of fitting a detection function.  However the choice of bins is subjective--there are no guidelines for how to do this.  In particular, using AIC comparisons for different binning choices or truncation distances is invalid, because AIC comparisons are only valid when exactly the same data are fitted to models.  There is also no mandate that all bins are of the same width.  I suspect a complete analysis of the data will likely truncate detections beyond, say 50m as those detections have little information about the shape of the detection function near the transect.

As you can see, there are many types of decisions associated with your questions, but little in the way of objective procedures to assist you. I'm willing to look at your histogram if you wish to send it to me off-list.

messages.subject_clean: Having enough sightings to fit a detection function that includes a covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

At my peril, I was wondering if any advice existed (preferably that I could reference) about how to approach the problem of having enough sightings to fit a detection function that includes a covariate, or multiple covariates. An approach that is probably desired by many people would be some general rule similar to the “60-80 rule” in Buckland et al. (2001), e.g. “we recommend at least X number of sightings per covariate included, with at least Y per level of each categorical covariate.” If such simple rules exist and are viewed as being reliable, then that’s great. But, given my impression that the community has applied the “60-80 rule” much more like a Holy Commandment than was originally intended, I am guessing that distance sampling experts will be very reluctant to give any similar advice regarding covariates.

More likely, you will want to explain that including covariates is a process or craft involving various considerations and tradeoffs, such as comparing goodness of fit in various ways, etc. That’s also great. But has anyone attempted to articulate their process in written form anywhere?

Thanks very much for any pointers you can provide,

Jason

Jason, yes, I’m always reluctant to give cookbook rules for the reason you state.  However, the basic recommendation of 60-80 sightings for line transect sampling (or perhaps 80-100 for point transect sampling) still holds as you add covariates.  By adding covariates, you have very little influence on variance – indeed, by modelling more variation, variance can reduce.  Of course, you note the issue of factor-type covariates.  If your goal is simply to estimate overall abundance, then again, the 60-80 rule is fine.  But if you have an interest in estimating density or abundance at each level of a factor, then you will get poor precision for factor levels with low numbers of detections.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

Thanks very much for your answer. I very much appreciate that you and the other developers of this methodology make a concerted effort to support the user community by answering our questions.

I guess I was wondering whether there could be a problem if many covariates were included in a model when only a “small” number of sightings are available. Taking the basic recommendation of 60-80, could there be problems if, say, 3 or 5 covariates were included, simply on the basis of having that many?

AIC is a popular way to compare candidate models. Would it be reasonable to leverage AIC to decide whether to rule out an additional covariate in these “small number of sightings” scenarios? (Of course, if AIC showed sufficient improvement after adding a covariate, one must still look at other diagnostics to ensure the resulting model did not show problems.)

Regarding the factor covariates, I have noted at least one extreme case in which a factor-level problem percolated into the overall abundance estimate. This example concerns dolphins observed on U.S. NOAA shipboard surveys off the southeast U.S. that used 25x binoculars. Plots and summary output appear below my signature. After truncation, 518 sightings remained. I fitted a hazard rate detection function and added Beaufort wind scale as a covariate. The resulting plots looked ok, except there were only a handful of sightings at Beaufort 0, that, when plotted, showed detection probability falling to only 0.9 out to 5000 m. This may or may not be realistic, and I made a note to follow up with observers to see what they thought about it.

But when I looked at the summary output, there was a clear problem: the Beaufort6 level had an SE of 2114. Looking into the data, there was only a single sighting with Beaufort 6. I had neglected to look at my histograms of covariates before fitting the models, so I didn’t catch this prior to fitting the model. (And I had been even more careless: I actually intended to discard effort at such high Beaufort, but failed to do so.) In any case, the extreme SE of this one sighting was carried into the final estimates of p and N, resulting in a CV of 4 for them.

On the basis of this example, I can fairly confidently recommend that it is a bad idea to include a categorical covariate with a level that has only *one* sighting. But how about 2, or 5, or 10? I don’t think I could recommend a minimum, at least at this stage of my experience. I suspect more seasoned analysts, particularly those with proper statistical training, might have some minimum, greater than 1, that they consider “common sense”. It would be nice to know such a number, for the convenience of automatically bounding the possibilities to investigate, or catching what happened here. But I completely understand any reluctance to offer basic rules of that kind. Fortunately, it seems possible to catch these problems in the summary diagnostics.

I guess my final worry, then, would be that such a problem would not be caught by summary diagnostics, leaving novice analysts to flounder, while seasoned analysts would avoid them by applying their own basic rules ahead of time. In that case, it would benefit the community if these unarticulated basic rules made it into the diagnostics, or at least were articulated somewhere.

Jason, yes, I’m always reluctant to give cookbook rules for the reason you state.  However, the basic recommendation of 60-80 sightings for line transect sampling (or perhaps 80-100 for point transect sampling) still holds as you add covariates. Hi folks,

At my peril, I was wondering if any advice existed (preferably that I could reference) about how to approach the problem of having enough sightings to fit a detection function that includes a covariate, or multiple covariates. An approach that is probably desired by many people would be some general rule similar to the “60-80 rule” in Buckland et al. (2001), e.g. “we recommend at least X number of sightings per covariate included, with at least Y per level of each categorical covariate.” If such simple rules exist and are viewed as being reliable, then that’s great. But, given my impression that the community has applied the “60-80 rule” much more like a Holy Commandment than was originally intended, I am guessing that distance sampling experts will be very reluctant to give any similar advice regarding covariates.

More likely, you will want to explain that including covariates is a process or craft involving various considerations and tradeoffs, such as comparing goodness of fit in various ways, etc. That’s also great. But has anyone attempted to articulate their process in written form anywhere?

Thanks very much for any pointers you can provide,

Jason

Jason

Always good to examine the estimated parameters of a fitted detection function (and their precision) before making inference from such a model.  Not only was there a giant SE in the Beaufort6 parameter estimate, but all the other covariate parameter SEs were roughly equal to the magnitude of the point estimates.  Note also in you (artistic) detection function plot, all detections other than Beaufort0 and 1 lie atop one another.  That's indicative of no demonstrable difference in detectability (according to the model) between states 2-6.  If I were to have seen this plot and table, I would have looked further into the ddf  object to look for a convergence failure result$ddf$ds$converge .  A non-zero value indicates a problem.  For this data set, the parameters are (nearly) non-identifiable perhaps because of the strong Beaufort0 and 1 effects; the optimiser is trying to resolve 5 more parameters from nearly identical shapes of the detection function in those states.

So it isn't just number of detections per covariate level that will keep you awake at night wondering if your models are appropriate.  Afraid that's why modelling cannot be fully automated.

Just a late afternoon idea. Please ignore if not relevant - or if such a resource already exists!

Mark

Jason, yes, I would use AIC to ensure you don’t include lots of covariates that add little but imprecision to the model.  I imagine your Beaufort 0 contribution to overall abundance is small, and the effect on variance small.  But yes, your Beaufort 6 contribution would be problematic.  In workshops, I have tended to say that you should aim for 60-80 observations per detection function model.  Whether you can get useful results from smaller samples depends on luck – in that odd patterns in the data that arise by chance with small samples can have a large effect on estimates.  The same would be true of estimates for levels of a factor with very few observations.  I would try to avoid the problem by combining factor levels where necessary, and would see if estimation is sensitive to whether or not I combine factor levels.  In your example, because you estimate that you detect most schools at sea state zero, you get a low estimate with small variance, causing no problems.  But if detectability is estimated to be very low in a stratum, you would hit problems.  So for stratum sea state 6, you would want appreciably more observations than for sea state 0.  Given this dependence, and other issues, it is hard to come up with cookbook rules that are likely to be always safe …

Steve

Hi Steve,

Thanks very much for your answer. I very much appreciate that you and the other developers of this methodology make a concerted effort to support the user community by answering our questions.

I guess I was wondering whether there could be a problem if many covariates were included in a model when only a “small” number of sightings are available. Taking the basic recommendation of 60-80, could there be problems if, say, 3 or 5 covariates were included, simply on the basis of having that many?

AIC is a popular way to compare candidate models. Would it be reasonable to leverage AIC to decide whether to rule out an additional covariate in these “small number of sightings” scenarios? (Of course, if AIC showed sufficient improvement after adding a covariate, one must still look at other diagnostics to ensure the resulting model did not show problems.)

Regarding the factor covariates, I have noted at least one extreme case in which a factor-level problem percolated into the overall abundance estimate. This example concerns dolphins observed on U.S. NOAA shipboard surveys off the southeast U.S. that used 25x binoculars. Plots and summary output appear below my signature. After truncation, 518 sightings remained. I fitted a hazard rate detection function and added Beaufort wind scale as a covariate. The resulting plots looked ok, except there were only a handful of sightings at Beaufort 0, that, when plotted, showed detection probability falling to only 0.9 out to 5000 m. This may or may not be realistic, and I made a note to follow up with observers to see what they thought about it.

But when I looked at the summary output, there was a clear problem: the Beaufort6 level had an SE of 2114. Looking into the data, there was only a single sighting with Beaufort 6. I had neglected to look at my histograms of covariates before fitting the models, so I didn’t catch this prior to fitting the model. (And I had been even more careless: I actually intended to discard effort at such high Beaufort, but failed to do so.) In any case, the extreme SE of this one sighting was carried into the final estimates of p and N, resulting in a CV of 4 for them.

On the basis of this example, I can fairly confidently recommend that it is a bad idea to include a categorical covariate with a level that has only *one* sighting. But how about 2, or 5, or 10? I don’t think I could recommend a minimum, at least at this stage of my experience. I suspect more seasoned analysts, particularly those with proper statistical training, might have some minimum, greater than 1, that they consider “common sense”. It would be nice to know such a number, for the convenience of automatically bounding the possibilities to investigate, or catching what happened here. But I completely understand any reluctance to offer basic rules of that kind. Fortunately, it seems possible to catch these problems in the summary diagnostics.

I guess my final worry, then, would be that such a problem would not be caught by summary diagnostics, leaving novice analysts to flounder, while seasoned analysts would avoid them by applying their own basic rules ahead of time. In that case, it would benefit the community if these unarticulated basic rules made it into the diagnostics, or at least were articulated somewhere.

Thanks again,

Jason

Mark,

It is funny you say that, because that is actually what I am working on with some of the CREEM team and NOAA as part of the DenMod project <https://synergy.st-andrews.ac.uk/denmod/>. We are developing a wiki called “Questions Frequently Asked by Marine Mammal Density Surface Modelers”. In it, we have attempted to catalogue and answer a number of questions that have come up in our work at Duke and elsewhere. The intended focus is narrow relative to distance sampling’s wide applicability, but many of the questions that have come up are quite general, such as this stuff about covariates. We will announce the availability of this FAQ as a resource at the World Marine Mammal Conference in two weeks.

I must hasten to add, before I incur Steve’s or Eric’s wrath, that by no means would I quote them in the FAQ. I would end up discussing what I learned with Dave Miller, my main collaborator on this, and we would write up something ourselves, if we felt confident enough to address it. At most, I might link to this conversation in the Google Groups archive. But I am trying to avoid accidentally introducing any new “basic rules”, e.g. by linking to something that facilitates practices like “one time, Steve Buckland said X, so that’s what I’m (blindly) doing”. So I’m fairly reluctant to link in that way.

I would definitely welcome a broader FAQ-style resource maintained by CREEM or the wider community. I think the Distance Sampling books are quite good, and have advice on surprising amounts of minutiae like this. But there are always more questions, and there are no books on density surface modeling yet. The distance-sampling list is one of the main tools to fill those gaps. I think online FAQs are another tool, particularly for questions that come up repeatedly but are not covered in the books. If you are anyone are interested in reviewing and/or contributing to the one we are building, we would be happy to bring you onboard.

Best,
Jason

Thank you, Steve and Eric, for your additional thoughts.

Eric, I looked back at my code and it turns out I apparently was aware of the convergence check; my code included a stopifnot(model$ds$converge == 0) after the call to ddf(). Now I am recalling, vaguely, that ddf() might issue a warning for certain convergence failures but not raise an error, so I put the check in to force the script to stop if it happened... Anyway, I know now that this particular case did not failure to converge, despite the similarity in detectability in some of those factor levels.

Thanks for suggesting tweaks. It is always helpful to hear another modeler’s line of thinking. Your suggestion of doing further truncation is interesting. In this case, I would be reluctant to do that, despite having >500 sightings, because the results were going into a density surface model. To facilitate the fitting of that model, I would want to retain as many sightings as I reasonably could. Am I right in believing there to be a kind of tension between improving the detection function by truncating its tail, vs. improving the spatial model by giving it more non-zero segments to work with? (Keeping mind that a long tail of low detectability can also cause problems in the spatial model.)

Jason

I was going to mention the potential to simplify the model by reducing the number of Beaufort classes; I can't guess how well observers can a) differentiate between classes 2 and 3 to accurately record the correct state and b) how much difference in the detection function for the given species might exist between classes 2 and 3--that's a question for the field crew.

As an armchair quarterback (apropos of Thanksgiving weekend), based upon your second figure and summary table, I would suggest there isn't a discernable difference in detectability between classes 2-3 and 4-6, and a 2 class covariate would probably be adequate.  Of course you already have high precision in your estimate of p-hat, so further fiddling would just be pounding the dust.

If I were really being fussy, I'd consider stronger truncation (toward 3km, bringing g(3km) ~ 0.2) which might change the situation with respect to the covariate levels.
